families.s: HSE airbag and seat-belt pretensioner storage, handling and disposal guidance
families.t: UN classification, licensing, transport packaging, locked storage, heat and ignition separation, handling orientation, deployment and disposal
f: Airbags and pretensioners can cause physical injury or poisoning if handled incorrectly.
The supplier's UN hazard classification should be established before storage or handling.
A storage licence may be required for devices classified for transport as explosives.
Devices should normally remain in their supplied transport packaging while stored.
Storage should be secure, dry and separated from flammables, hot work and electrical ignition sources.
Manufacturer-specific procedures must be checked before work because vehicle systems differ.
An undeployed airbag should be carried with the trim cover facing away and should not be placed face down.
Deployment and disposal should only follow trained procedures and supplier advice; undeployed explosive devices must not enter ordinary waste.
families.g: Airbag and pretensioner risk depends on classification and packaging, storage quantity and location, heat and electrical exposure, handling orientation, vehicle procedure, training and disposal route.

families.s: HSE electric and hybrid vehicle high-voltage and stored-energy guidance
families.t: high voltage, retained charge, battery chemicals, fire and explosion, unexpected movement, silent operation, manufacturer information, tools and competence
f: Electric and hybrid vehicles contain voltages far above conventional 12 or 24 volt vehicle systems.
Contact with live high-voltage components can cause fatal electric shock.
Components may retain dangerous voltage after the vehicle has been switched off.
Battery systems store enough energy to create fire or explosion if mishandled.
Damaged batteries can release harmful liquids or explosive gases.
Electric motors or the vehicle can move unexpectedly, and quiet operation may reduce warning to nearby people.
Vehicle-specific manufacturer information is needed because electrical designs and isolation procedures differ.
Competence, specialist tools and controls must match whether the work is low risk, incident response, non-high-voltage repair or high-voltage-system work.
families.g: Electric-vehicle risk depends on vehicle design and voltage, isolation and retained energy, battery condition, movement and charging, task category, tools, manufacturer information and competence.

families.s: HSE motor-vehicle isocyanate spray-booth, clearance-time and respiratory-protection guidance
families.t: 2-pack paint, invisible mist, spray booth, clearance time, air-fed breathing apparatus, visor discipline, health surveillance and biological monitoring
f: Isocyanates in 2-pack vehicle paints are a major cause of occupational asthma and can also cause dermatitis.
Spraying produces substantial invisible mist that must be contained in the booth or spray room.
Spraying should not be carried out outside the controlled enclosure.
The booth or room clearance time should be measured and clearly communicated.
Air-fed breathing apparatus should be worn while spray mist remains present.
The sprayer should not lift the visor immediately after spraying while contaminated air may remain.
Spray booths, rooms and extraction systems require effective management and maintenance.
Regular health surveillance and suitable exposure or biological monitoring support verification of control.
families.g: Isocyanate-spraying risk depends on paint chemistry, spray method and quantity, booth containment and clearance time, RPE, maintenance, work practices, monitoring and worker susceptibility.

families.s: HSE motor-body preparation dust, hot-work fume and extraction guidance
families.t: powered sanding, fine dust, lead and coatings, welding fume, task segregation, on-tool extraction, local exhaust ventilation, cleaning and respiratory health
f: Powered discing and sanding during body preparation can release high concentrations of fine dust.
Some preparation work can involve lead or hazardous material from old coatings and fillers.
Body filling and preparation should be separated from other work to limit the number exposed.
Powered sanding should use tools with built-in extraction or suitable local exhaust ventilation.
Welding and flame cutting can release fumes from paint, primer, underseal and other vehicle coatings.
Mobile extraction should be positioned close to welding or cutting fume where practicable.
Local extraction is particularly important in confined locations and when welding stainless steel.
Cleaning methods should avoid redistributing settled hazardous dust into the workshop air.
families.g: Body-preparation risk depends on coating and substrate, sanding and hot-work method, dust and fume generation, segregation and extraction, cleaning, task duration, RPE and worker susceptibility.

families.s: HSE COSHH essentials for motor-vehicle cleaning, valeting and repair tasks
families.t: low-pressure washing, solvent valeting, concentrates, fuels, lubricants, degreasing, abrasive dust, battery charging, chemical storage and control systems
f: Motor-repair COSHH sheets provide task-specific good practice for cleaning and repair operations.
Cleaning guidance covers low-pressure washing, solvent-based valeting and dilution of chemical concentrates.
Repair guidance covers work with petrol, diesel and LPG fuels.
Separate controls are provided for lubricants, waste oil and small-scale solvent degreasing.
Abrasive-wheel work can create hazardous dust requiring exposure control.
Battery charging can release hazardous gases and requires suitable charging arrangements.
Vehicle exhaust fume in garages and warehouses needs specific controls.
Chemical products should be selected, stored and used with engineering controls, work practices and PPE appropriate to the task.
families.g: Motor-repair COSHH risk depends on product and process, quantity and frequency, exposure route, enclosure and ventilation, storage and transfer, cleaning, PPE and maintenance.
